newsitem.title: UK: Oil price rise fuelled by European freeze.
newsitem.headline: Oil price rise fuelled by European freeze.

text.p: Winter chills sent oil prices rising again on Monday as European buyers rushed to cover seasonal demand amid sub-zero temperatures.
London February futures for bellwether North Sea Brent Blend gained 26 cents to close at $23.68 a barrel, helped by renewed demand for heating oil in northern Europe in particular.

"I'm sure that gas oil (heating oil) has fuelled the move higher today with the severe winter weather we're seeing across the continent," said analyst Tim Holmes at brokerage Mees Pierson Derivatives.
January gas oil futures in London closed $6.00 a tonne firmer at $223.00.
Most of Europe spent Christmas gripped by freezing conditions which stretched as far south as the Mediterranean island of Corsica.
The mercury dipped as low as minus 30 degrees Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit) in the mountains of northern Italy and to -37C (-35F) in Poland.
"The cold weather has obviously helped gas oil," said a trader in London. "We're seeing good German buying."

Oil prices this year, at $20.30 for Brent running 20 percent higher than in 1995, have found strong support from a widespread western oil company policy of cutting costs by keeping inventory levels as low as possible.
Germany, easily Europe's biggest heating oil consumer, has been running on unusually thin inventories this winter, leaving prices vulnerable to sudden extra demand.
German household stocks of heating oil fell in November to about 62 percent of capacity, compared with 68 percent last year, German traders have estimated.
But dealers warned that prices were up in such a thinly traded market that an equally quick reverse could not be ruled out.
"I don't know if jumping on the move higher is necessarily a wise move," said a trader. "Unless the cold spell is fairly prolonged, I don't know how supportive this will be for Brent."

Unseasonally mild weather in the past few days in the northern eastern states of the United States, the world's single largest heating oil market, could put a damper on further price rises despite low stocks, dealers said.

Data released by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) and the American Petroleum Institute (API) last Thursday showed a hefty 5-6 million barrel weekly fall in U.S. crude oil stocks levels, to around 290 million barrels.
U.S. stocks of heating oil also fell by 1.5-2 million barrels. While this is a relatively small amount, it had a positive effect on prices because traders had been expecting a rise in stocks.
Oil markets so far have found little difficulty in absorbing limited volumes of Iraqi oil exports permitted under a United Nations oil-for-food exchange.

Iraq started exports on December 17 under one of 21 contracts for some 500,000 barrels a day of crude sales, enough at current prices to raise the $2 billion Iraq is allowed over a six-month period to pay for humanitarian needs.

"I think inventory levels, especially in the U.S., are still lean enough for the weather to be a key factor for a while yet, and stop Iraqi crude having a big impact," said Russell Hill, head trader at Austrian oil company OMV.
